blocks.text: Data Science
Data science is the process of collecting, organising, analysing, and interpreting data to find useful information and support decision-making.
Structured and Unstructured Data
Structured data is arranged in a fixed format, such as tables with rows and columns. Unstructured data does not follow a fixed format, such as images, videos, emails, and audio files.
Machine Learning
Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence in which computers learn patterns from data and use them to make predictions or decisions.
Supervised Learning
Supervised learning is a machine learning method in which the model learns from labelled data, such as study hours and known exam scores.
Unsupervised Learning
Unsupervised learning is a machine learning method in which the model finds hidden patterns or groups in data without labelled outputs.
Reinforcement Learning
Reinforcement learning is a learning method in which an agent learns by taking actions and receiving rewards or penalties.
Feature and Target Value
A feature is an input value used by a model, such as study hours or attendance. A target value is the output the model tries to predict, such as an exam score.
Train-Test Split
Train-test split is the process of dividing data into training data for teaching the model and testing data for checking its performance.
Predictive Model
A predictive model uses past data to estimate future values or outcomes.
Model Evaluation
Model evaluation is the process of checking how well a machine learning model performs using measures such as accuracy, error, precision, recall, and F1-score.
Parameter Tuning
Parameter tuning is the process of adjusting model settings to improve its performance.
Prediction
Prediction is the process of estimating a future value or event based on past data.
Causality
Causality explains cause-and-effect relationships between variables and helps identify why something happens.
Machine Learning Tools
Machine learning tools are software platforms used to analyse data and build models. Common examples include Excel, R, Python, and Jupyter Notebook.
